Malaysia Women's T20I Tri-Series, 2026 Malaysia Women vs Indonesia Women 1st Match Sandpapergate 'Betrayed' Bancroft angered by Cummins' denial, says whole team knew of sandpaper plan
 by Cricbuzz Staff •     Share Tweet Bancroft was suspended for 9 months for his role in the controversy. © Getty Bancroft was suspended for 9 months for his role in the controversy. © Getty Cameron Bancroft has said that the entire Australian team knew he was using sandpaper on the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa. In doing so, he has backed Usman Khawaja’s account of the scandal and said he felt betrayed and angered by Pat Cummins’ denials last week.
 In a piece published in The West Australian on Wednesday (November 18), Bancroft admitted he did not give a “complete and truthful” account when Cricket Australia investigated him in 2018. He said he held back key details about when the use of sandpaper began, how long it continued, and how much the rest of the touring party knew in order to not implicate others.
 "It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone," Bancroft wrote of Cummins’ denial in a recent press conference. “It was not just the three of us - Steve Smith, David Warner and I - who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.
 “I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.”
 Bancroft is now the third member of that touring party to come forward since Khawaja’s book, Sabr, reopened the eight-year-old episode. Cummins called Khawaja’s claims “utter nonsense” in a lengthy presser while Warner sided with Khawaja. On Sunday, Chadd Sayers, who was 12th man in Cape Town, told SEN that he carried the sandpaper off the field himself with the drinks after Tea. He said the plan had already been in motion in Port Elizabeth a week earlier, that he believed “everyone knew”, and that CA never interviewed him.
 Bancroft said the “final straw” in opening up was Cummins' press conference on Friday. There, the current Test captain repeated his long-held position that he and the rest of the bowling attack did not know sandpaper was being used in Cape Town. "What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this," Bancroft wrote.
 “My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019. But I have reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.”
 Bancroft also clarified that the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine were in constant conversations with him about how the ball was reverse swinging. “We did this together for the bowlers especially, but more widely the team and to win the game,” he wrote.
 “I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to.I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough.”
 He also recalled the mood on the field as the wickets came.
 “I remember Mitchell Marsh taking wickets and joking about how much the ball was swinging and how he never used to swing it like that. There was laughter and celebrations when wickets fell.
 “I was amazed that sandpaper could have such an effect on a cricket ball. I was stoked my impact was leading to the team doing well.”
 Bancroft also confirmed earlier reports that Warner raised the idea of using sandpaper but said he could not do it himself, because he feared the cameras that were following him closely would catch him given his reputation. CA’s 2018 investigation had also found that Warner raised the idea.
 According to Bancroft, the plan was discussed in a “wider team environment”. He said head coach Darren Lehmann and bowling mentor David Saker were both present when the group agreed to it. Smith, as Bancroft remembers it, joined the conversation briefly before making it clear he “wanted no part in it”.
 “I remember being warned to be careful, and others suggesting they would not do it if they were in my position,” he wrote. “I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised. I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating. But I also saw an opportunity to contribute.”
 Bancroft was banned from all cricket for nine months after he was caught using sandpaper on the ball in the infamous Cape Town Test, as Australia tried to get more reverse swing. Smith, then captain, and Warner were each suspended for 12 months by Cricket Australia and barred from leadership roles.
 Later in the day, CA acknowledged Bancroft's statement, adding: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.
 "We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events. We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."
